newsitem.title: CUBA: Clinton's Cuba move gained him little thanks - Cuba.
newsitem.headline: Clinton's Cuba move gained him little thanks - Cuba.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's move to suspend for another six months implementation of part of the controversial Helms-Burton law has won him scant thanks, Cuban parliamentary president Ricardo Alarcon said on Friday.
Speaking in an interview on state television, Alarcon said that the highest praise Clinton's decision got from abroad appeared to have been that it was positive, but not enough.

Helms-Burton, which reinforced Washington's 35-year-old economic embargo against Havana, was enacted last March. It includes provisions to punish third country firms investing in Cuba that have been strongly condemned by U.S. allies such as Mexico, Canada and the European Union.

Last week Clinton suspended for a further six months implentation of Title Three, under which U.S. citizens may sue foreign firms seen benefiting from property nationalised by Cuba after President Fidel Castro's 1959 revolution.
"The only thing Clinton can do, poor thing, is suspend every six months the possibility that a foreign investor is taken to court," Alarcon said.
He said international pressure and the impracticality of implementing these parts of the law would likely force Washington to dump Title Three and Title Four of the law.

Under Title Four, which has been applied against a Mexican telecommuncations firm and a Canadian mining company, executives of firms deemed to be "trafficking" in expropriated property may be barred entry to the United States.
But Alarcon said the law would still be unacceptable to Cuba if its Titles One and Two remained in effect.

The first two chapters codify the existing U.S. embargo and present a blueprint for change in Cuba, in which improved relations between Washington and Havana are conditional on a complete overhaul of the political system. Alarcon described Title Two as a plan for how to take over Cuba.
